title: Keyword Parsing vs. Requirement Extraction for Federal RFPs
summary: Keyword scans for shall, will and must miss RFP requirements written other ways. See where compliance matrices break and how to extract the rest.
body_markdown:
Keyword parsing gives you a compliance matrix fast, but not a complete one. Plenty of binding requirements in a federal solicitation never use 'shall,' 'will,' or 'must' at all, and a word-match scan passes over them without a flag. If you're building your matrix from that output alone, you're responding to a partial picture of what evaluators will score you against.


**TLDR:**


- Keyword parsing flags "shall," "will," and "must" but misses passive-voice PWS obligations, declarative Section L rules, and Section M scoring language written without those words.
- Agencies can eliminate a proposal over a format rule; GAO backed the Labor Department when it eliminated a proposal over its font (B-423202, 2025).
- Requirement extraction reads Sections C, L, and M together, using document structure and cross-references between sections, not trigger words alone.
- Treat each amendment as a reason to re-shred the sections it changes; acknowledging it without updating the compliance matrix leaves changed requirements unanswered.
- GovEagle generates a compliance matrix from Sections L and M and the PWS or SOW, quoting each requirement word for word with its source; after an amendment, ask GovEagle to rebuild the matrix and outline.


## What Keyword Parsing Actually Does in RFP Review


Keyword parsing is a scan of the solicitation document for trigger words like "shall," "will," and "must" that signal a compliance obligation. Every sentence containing one of those words gets flagged, extracted, and dropped into a compliance matrix row.


Large federal RFPs often run past 100 pages once Sections C, L, and M, attachments, and amendments are counted. When a proposal team has 72 hours to produce a compliant matrix, a rule-based word match gets something on the page fast. Tools like VisibleThread built rule-based shreds around this logic.


The problem is that keyword parsing was never designed to catch everything.


### Where the Logic Breaks Down


Plenty of binding or scored requirements never use modal verbs at all.[Section M](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/section-m-evaluation-factors-for-award) criteria written without "will," performance standards embedded in a[PWS](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/pws-performance-work-statement) , and submission format rules described in declarative sentences all carry real compliance weight without triggering a word-match scan. A keyword parser passes over them, leaving gaps that surface at Red Team or, worse, during evaluation.


## Why "Shall," "Will," and "Must" Don't Cover the Full Requirement Set


Federal solicitations express obligations in far more ways than three modal verbs can capture. Evaluation criteria in Section M often read like "Technical Approach is more important than Past Performance" or "Outstanding: Proposal indicates an exceptional approach and understanding of the requirements." Neither line contains "shall," "will," or "must," yet both carry direct scoring consequences under[FAR 15.305(a)](https://www.acquisition.gov/far/15.305) (15.202(a)(1) in the FAR Overhaul), which requires agencies to assess proposals solely on the factors and subfactors in the solicitation. A parser does flag Section M lines that say "will," such as "The Government will consider the offeror's staffing approach," but a keyword match on its own doesn't show which[Section L](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/section-l-instructions-conditions-and-notices-to-bidders) instruction a line pairs with or the weight Section M gives it.


The same blind spot appears across solicitation structures:


- Section L submission instructions phrased as declaratives ("each volume includes a table of contents") read as formatting notes but function as compliance checkboxes evaluators verify.
- PWS task areas written in passive voice ("support services are provided on-site") carry performance obligations that never surface in a modal verb scan.
- Preference language like "offerors are encouraged to provide" signals scoring differentiation that a keyword parser skips.


A proposal team that builds its compliance matrix from that scan submits a response with gaps that evaluators score against.


## Where Keyword Parsing Fails Across RFP Sections


The failure pattern runs consistently across the[uniform contract format](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/ucf-uniform-contract-format) , though it surfaces differently in each section.


RFP Section Typical Phrasing That Gets Missed Proposal Risk


Section C (PWS/SOW) Deliverables listed as passive-voice performance standards Task obligations missing from the technical volume


Section L "Resumes are limited to two pages," "Volumes are organized by factor" Page limits, font rules, and attachment instructions treated as optional


Section M "Outstanding: Proposal indicates an exceptional approach," order-of-importance language Scoring discriminators never mapped to a response section


Amendments / Q&As Q&A answers that bind like amendments Requirement changes invisible to tools scanning only the original file


A keyword pass on the base RFP alone misses changes that arrive later in attachments, amendments, and Q&A answers, so each of those files needs its own pass.


## What Is RFP Requirement Extraction?


Requirement extraction starts from a different question than keyword parsing. A parser asks: does this sentence contain a trigger word? Extraction asks: what does the government actually need to see covered in this proposal, and where will evaluators score it?


Extraction reads Section M alongside Section L, because a submission instruction in Section L only tells you what to submit. Section M tells you what separates an outstanding rating from an acceptable one. A[compliance matrix](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/compliance-matrix) built without connecting them leaves proposal writers responding to requirements with no understanding of their relative weight.


Structural context carries as much interpretive weight as individual sentences. A deliverable described in the PWS carries an implicit performance obligation even in passive voice. A subfactor weighting table in Section M signals scoring priority without using any modal verb. Extraction treats document position, heading hierarchy, and cross-references between sections as interpretive signals, because an evaluator scoring a proposal uses that same context when deciding what a response adequately covers.


The output is a requirement set where every item traces back to something the government intends to score.


## The Compliance Cost of Missed Requirements


Missed requirements carry costs that vary by where they surface in the evaluation sequence.[GAO holds](https://www.gao.gov/assets/890/885528.pdf) that a proposal that fails to conform to a material solicitation requirement "is technically unacceptable and cannot form the basis for award." Format rules count too: in[Horizons Youth Services](https://www.gao.gov/products/b-423202) (B-423202, 2025), GAO found the Labor Department reasonably eliminated a proposal over its font.


Requirements that reach the technical volume but get thin answers carry a different cost:[scoring gaps](https://www.goveagle.com/blog/technical-volume-common-gaps) . An evaluator rating against Section M subfactors scores what the proposal shows, not what the contractor intended. Thin answers become weaknesses. A material requirement left out becomes a deficiency, which can make the proposal unawardable.


Amendment acknowledgment failures add another layer. In[Morrish-Wallace Construction](https://www.gao.gov/products/b-423796.2) (B-423796.2, Feb. 2026), a sealed-bid construction case, GAO upheld a protest because the low bidder never acknowledged an amendment that changed a key structural spec. McCarter & English's[Government Contracts Law blog](https://www.governmentcontractslaw.com/2026/03/spring-cleaning-your-proposals-gaos-latest-reminder-that-compliance-is-critical/) called it a reminder that "a single compliance miss can be outcome determinative." A matrix that never picked up that amendment would have missed the new spec too.

## How RFP Amendments Compound the Parsing Problem


Amendments can arrive late in the cycle and can change the sections that carry the most compliance weight. For example:


- [Amendment 0001](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/amendment) revises Section L page limits.
- Amendment 0002 deletes a PWS task area.
- Amendment 0003 reframes an evaluation subfactor based on industry questions.


Each change touches requirements the original keyword scan already processed and filed away.


A static compliance matrix built at RFP release does not update itself. Teams working from that original scan respond to requirements that may have since changed or been removed, and miss obligations introduced by the amendment. The subtler risk is a team that formally acknowledges an amendment without re-shredding it for changed requirements.


Q&A responses compound the problem further. Contracting officers frequently answer industry questions in ways that clarify or narrow what a compliant response must include. Those answers often sit in a separate Q&A file, but[GAO treats Q&As](https://www.gao.gov/products/b-422938,b-422938.2) published to all offerors as part of the solicitation. A keyword pass scoped to the original file never sees them.


## Building a Requirement Extraction Framework for Your Team


Reliable RFP shredding and requirement extraction take three passes through the solicitation.


The first pass covers Section L alone: every submission instruction, format rule, and volume requirement logged with its exact source location. The second covers Section C and any attached PWS or SOW, pulling deliverables, performance standards, and reporting obligations regardless of phrasing. The third treats Section M as an extraction target in its own right, with each subfactor logged as a requirement and weighted by the relative importance Section M states.


After those three passes, review every attachment, Q&A response, and amendment separately. These sit in separate files and get missed when teams treat them as reference material.


Each extracted requirement should capture four fields:


- Source section, so reviewers can trace any requirement back to its origin in the RFP without re-reading the full document.
- Verbatim text, preserving the exact language instead of a paraphrase that may strip qualifying conditions.
- Proposal response location, mapping the requirement to the section of your submission that answers it.
- Assigned owner, so accountability is explicit before the first draft is written.


Fill in all four fields before drafting starts. After each amendment, re-shred the affected sections and update these fields.


## How AI Changes the Requirement Extraction Calculation


AI reads solicitation language for its meaning, so it isn't limited to trigger words. Where a keyword parser skips "Technical Approach is more important than Past Performance," an AI model reading the whole solicitation can recognize it as scoring language and record it. It can also read attachments, amendments, and Q&A answers alongside the base document, so a re-shred takes less work.


The edge cases still require human review. Three situations where AI extraction produces a candidate requirement in place of a confirmed one:


- Ambiguous PWS task areas where the scope boundary depends on interpretation, not explicit language.
- Implied obligations rooted in agency-specific acquisition history that no solicitation text makes explicit.
- Requirements that only make sense read against a prior contract's SOW.


A proposal manager needs to verify those flagged items before they enter the compliance matrix as settled obligations. AI output needs a check too, because a model can miss a requirement; a matrix that quotes each requirement word for word with its source makes that check fast. AI narrows the gap between what the solicitation says and what the compliance matrix captures. Closing it entirely still requires a human who understands what the government is actually trying to buy.

## Final Thoughts


A compliance matrix built on keyword parsing looks complete until an evaluator finds the gaps your parser skipped. Section M subfactors, passive-voice PWS obligations, and amendment changes still get scored whether or not your tool flagged them, so build the matrix from the whole solicitation and check it before Red Team does.


## FAQ


### What's the difference between keyword parsing and true requirement extraction for federal RFPs?


Keyword parsing scans solicitation text for modal verbs like "shall," "will," and "must" to flag compliance obligations. True requirement extraction reads document position, heading hierarchy, and cross-section relationships, treating Section M evaluation subfactors, passive-voice PWS deliverables, and declarative Section L formatting instructions as compliance obligations regardless of whether they contain trigger words. The practical gap is that keyword parsing misses scored evaluation factors and submission rules that never use modal verbs, producing a compliance matrix with structural gaps that evaluators score against.


### How do I build a compliance matrix that captures requirements across Sections C, L, and M without missing scored evaluation factors?


Run three separate passes: Section L first for submission instructions and format rules, Section C and attached PWS for deliverables and performance standards, then Section M as a standalone extraction target where each subfactor is logged as a requirement, weighted by the relative importance Section M states. After those passes, review every attachment, amendment, and Q&A response separately, as these sit in separate files and carry requirement changes that a single initial shred misses. Each extracted requirement should log its source section, verbatim text, proposal response location, and assigned owner before drafting begins.


### Can AI tools reliably replace manual RFP shredding for federal proposal compliance matrices?


AI tools can surface scored evaluation factors and passive-voice obligations that keyword parsers skip, and they can read amendments and Q&A answers alongside the base document. Three situations still require human review before a candidate requirement enters the matrix as a confirmed obligation: ambiguous PWS task areas where scope depends on interpretation, implied obligations rooted in agency-specific acquisition history, and requirements that only make sense read against a prior contract's SOW. AI narrows the gap between what the solicitation says and what the matrix captures; closing it entirely requires a human who understands what the government is trying to buy.

Look for a tool that quotes each requirement word for word with its source, covers Sections L and M and the PWS or SOW, and works inside Word and Excel.
